title: Why Your Preschooler's Hitting, Biting, or Kicking Isn't Bad Behavior—It's a Bid for Bodily Autonomy
dek: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to shout, "I have no say"—when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior will decrease.
why: Most approaches repeat "no hitting" and add punishment, without touching the need behind the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal and demonstrates scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.
who: Parents whose child just started preschool and who get frequent calls from the teacher; and preschool teachers who want to reduce aggression in their classroom without relying on punishment.
skip: After 16:57 it's a course pitch; if you only want the methods, you can skip it.

points.h: Hitting is a child's cry that their body isn't their own
points.body: Preschool is often the first place where a child is controlled by an adult other than their parents in nearly every bodily arrangement: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and move. In the previous three years, they could largely decide when to run and when to go to the bathroom. Sitting on the carpet for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old lacks the language to assert "my body, my rules," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools left. So when you get that call from the teacher, don't rush to scold "keep your hands to yourself." Instead ask: how much say did this child have over their own life before this, and what can you give back now?

points.h: Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
points.body: Teachers often say that a high proportion of children at a certain preschool are kindergarten-ready, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: when the teacher says sit, you sit, even if you're in the middle of something, even if your body is overloaded. Parents worry that if the child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, college, or good life. But the price the child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either; they themselves need competence, child safety, ease, and even a sense of power. Many entered education to repair their own childhood trauma, but only know how to use a power-over model of relationship. Seeing both sides' situations opens up room for negotiation.

points.h: We accommodate ourselves but refuse to accommodate our children
points.body: When adults attend a party and feel overloaded, we arrive early, leave early, retreat to a quiet room, or even wear noise-canceling earplugs—we find this natural. But when it comes to children, except for routine things like extended test time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive in the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodations than they allow their children. The original provides a concrete image: a bigger, stronger adult picks you up without explanation from a quiet room and carries you back to the middle of a noisy party—if it happened to an adult, you'd immediately see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we turn a blind eye.

points.h: The fix lies before the behavior, not in the behavior itself
points.body: Repeating "no hitting" doesn't work because that's not the knowledge the child lacks. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before the bite? What else happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who loses control when pushed in line—let them stand at the front, back, or outside the line. A child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. Analogy to adults: when your partner snaps at you in the evening for no apparent reason, it's often not about what they said in the moment, but about a morning argument, lack of sleep, and a cascade of stress. If the other person then says "your attitude needs work," you'd explode too; yet we often only do the latter to our children.

points.h: Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, listen to the 'no'
points.body: Telling the teacher "please change your approach" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer way in is to set aside judgment and reconstruct the facts: don't ask who's responsible, just ask what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you've figured out whether the trigger is sensory or about autonomy, then empathize with the three things behind the teacher's behavior: competence, the children's safety, and the need for a breather. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "Can the child sit on a ball outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal, but what need that 'no' is still protecting, and find a way that meets both needs simultaneously.

points.h: A nap-time conflict resolved without winners or losers
points.body: Jen's daughter Carys, at age three, couldn't nap. The teacher required her to lie down; she was bored and frustrated—her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state regulations required providing a nap, and nap time was also the teacher's break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could play quietly with soft toys that didn't roll, while the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the break, and Jen escaped the dilemma of tattletale calls. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is preserved.

points.h: All methods boil down to one question
points.body: Compress all the above methods into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and instead ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are just surface signals; the real message might be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meet it can be designed; and it's almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

terms.def: A basic need to have choice over one's life and body and to act according to one's own will.
A metric used in early childhood education to measure a child's maturity in sitting still, following instructions, and adapting to group rules.
A change to the environment, rules, or arrangements to match an individual's sensory or other needs.
An interaction pattern where the adult occupies a superior position and treats the child with commands and domination, as opposed to a collaborative model.

quotes.text: hitting or kicking can be one of the only tools that a three or four-year-old has for saying I don't have any say over what happens to my body right now and I need some of that.
When we imagine it happening to an adult we can kind of see it's an obvious violation of that person's body autonomy. And it is for a child too, it's just that we don't see it that way.
Being kindergarten ready means the child has learned that they are to do what an adult says even if that goes against what they know is right for their body.

But when we think about accommodations for kids unless it's for something like more time when they're taking a test we worry that they won't be able to survive in the real world if we accommodate them too much.
We know that we want that for ourselves, but somehow when kids are involved, we only focus on the behavior that we don't want to see and how do we change that?
And if the teacher says no, which they may do, what you're really listening for is what need they're trying to meet that underlies that no.
What need is this behavior communicating? Because from there you can find strategies to meet everyone's needs.
